title: Hubble peers through the looking glass
caption: The galaxy cluster LCDCS 0829, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: LCDCS 0829 · constellation Virgo · about z=0.451 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Strange arcs curve around the galaxy cluster LCDCS-0829. They are images of more distant galaxies, stretched by the cluster's own enormous mass, which acts like a giant magnifying glass. The effect is called gravitational lensing.

Lensing follows from Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity. The mass of the cluster bends the fabric of the Universe, and light from background galaxies travels along that bend. As well as making some objects look bigger and brighter, lensing can create several images of one galaxy and pull them into arcs.

The cluster's odd name comes from the Las Campanas Distant Clusters Survey, carried out in March 1995 with a 1-metre telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile. By scanning a long, narrow strip of the southern sky, it found more than one thousand galaxy clusters, most of them previously unknown.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used three filters. Blue light (F475W) is shown in blue, near-infrared light (F814W) in green, and longer-wavelength infrared (F850LP) in red.
understand.eye: Much of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the lensed arcs are far too faint to see without Hubble's long exposures.

explore: This deep image combines 36 exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with a total of 5280 s per filter. The picture spans about 2.8 arcminutes.
alt: A galaxy cluster with thin, curved arcs of light from lensed background galaxies.
